Bertrand's Paradox

GeometryCirclesProbability
Game: Drag a line across the circle and see how often it is longer than a side of the triangle drawn inside.
How to play: Drag the three dots, choose how the next lines are picked, then press Draw or Draw 100. There is no winning — just watch the numbers.
Look for the math

One question — how long is a chord picked at random? — gives three different answers. Which one you get depends on what you mean by "at random". That is the Bertrand paradox.

The question and the three answers

The old page asks: given a circle, find the probability that a chord chosen at random is longer than the side of an inscribed equilateral triangle. It gives three answers: 1/3, 1/4 and 1/2. Take the radius to be 1: the triangle's side is then √3 and the longest chord, the diameter, is 2. (The old page prints a bare "3" in one sentence because its square-root image was lost; its red line and the applet both use √3.)

Fixing one end

Pick two points on the rim and join them, or keep one end fixed and pick only the other. Either way, if the angle between the two ends is t, the chord is 2·sin(t/2). That is longer than √3 exactly when t > 2π/3. With one end held still, the free end must land in one third of the circle, so the chance is 1/3. The logic test walks 720 equally spaced positions of the free end and confirms this; it also confirms the page's claim that the two simulations have the same distribution.

Looking at the midpoint instead

A chord is also fixed by its midpoint M: it runs straight across, at right angles to the line from the centre to M. Its length is 2√(1−|M|²), so it is long exactly when |M| < 1/2. If M is spread evenly over the area of the circle, the favourable part is a circle of half the radius, with 1/4 of the area. If instead |M| is spread evenly from 0 to 1, the favourable part is half the radii, giving 1/2. The page also says the favourable third of the endpoint arc sweeps 1/4 of the disc while the rest sweeps 3/4, a ratio of 1:3 rather than 1:2; the logic test's grid over the disc bears that out.

Reading the graph

Each button draws chords the way the applet's SHOULDFIX option did: two random ends, one fixed end, a random radius, or a random spot. The line on the right is the running chance that a chord is no longer than a given length; the dashed red marker sits at √3, and its height is the chance of a short chord. Over 30,000 trials the four options approach 2/3, 2/3, 1/2, 3/4 there, the complements of the page's three answers. The long chords are green, short ones dark, so the two cases are easy to tell apart; nothing is won or lost in this illustration.

Try Draw 100 with one fixed end, then with a random spot. The graph settles near the same place for the first two options but not for the last two.
